newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow firm on NATO as Albright starts talks.
newsitem.headline: Moscow firm on NATO as Albright starts talks.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday began talks in Moscow intended to ease Russian opposition to NATO's eastward expansion but the Kremlin made clear she faced a tough task winning over her hosts.

Russian news agencies said Albright had met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, who have both conducted a campaign against NATO's plans to admit former Warsaw Pact countries.

Details of their discussions were not immediately available, but the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's enlargement plans were sure to dominate two days of talks which culminate in a meeting on Friday with President Boris Yeltsin.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said before Albright arrived that Russia remained implacably opposed to NATO expansion, which it regards as a threat to its security.
"(Our opposition) will remain, whatever the outcome of the negotiations between Russia and the Atlantic alliance," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

In a front-page article in the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily, Boris Berezovsky, deputy secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council, said NATO's plan was as dangerous for the West as for Russia because it re-divided Europe into two camps.

"It is above all a decision by the West that Russia cannot be integrated...It is a totally aggressive decision with regard to Russia that is also exceptionally dangerous for the West itself," said Berezovsky, also an influential businessman.

The foreign ministers of Italy and Germany, who have both visited the capital of their former Cold War foe this week trying to sell NATO's plans, found a rare unanimity among Russians across the political spectrum over the issue.

"NATO is an instrument of the Cold War and we have only just learned to live without the Cold War," the communist speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament, Gennady Seleznyov, told Italy's Lamberto Dini on Thursday.
During a joint news conference with Dini, Primakov said: "Russia has a negative position on NATO expansion and will continue to hold this position."
Dini sounded a conciliatory note, saying Italy believed NATO expansion could "only take place with the consensus of Russia, and not against its will".

He said he was confident that NATO and Russia could reach agreement on the issue by the time of the alliance's July summit in Madrid when it is expected to invite several countries, including Poland and Hungary, to join.
Yastrzhembsky repeated the Kremlin's demand for a legally binding contract providing security guarantees for Russia in the event of NATO's expansion.
"The signing of a legally binding document between Russia and NATO is meant to reduce to a minimum the unavoidable negative consequences of the bloc's expansion," he said.

"The conclusion of such a document would be not a gift to Russia but a demonstration of healthy pragmatism by the Western countries, based on their understanding of their own interests of national security."

NATO wants closer ties with Russia, which it recognises as an indispensable part of any future European security arrangement, but is reluctant to sign any document that would give Moscow an effective veto over its decision-making.
During her visit Albright is expected to outline several new initiatives, including the offer of a joint NATO-Russia military brigade, mainly to be used in peacekeeping.

Albright, who also had talks with Russian Orthodox Patriarch Alexiy II, is expected to explain sweeping changes to a landmark arms control treaty agreed by NATO allies on Wednesday in another bid to win Moscow round.

The changes to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty take account of several Russian objections to existing ceilings on arsenals, which Moscow says are rooted in the Cold War and put it at a disadvantage.
